pr_body:
- Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/34449 (System.Text.Json.Serialization.JsonStringEnumConverter isn't linker-safe)
- Adds annotations to make simple serializer usages linker safe (e.g. deserializing most collections and POCOs with primitive members). More complex object graphs e.g. POCOs with POCO properties will probably need [`DynamicallyAccessedMemberTypes.RecursiveProperties/Constructors`](https://github.com/mono/linker/issues/1087).
    - @steveharter mentions another view point/approach in https://github.com/mono/linker/issues/1087#issuecomment-615479254.

Deserializing immutable collections is not linker safe - will address with https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/38593.

issue_context.title: System.Text.Json.Serialization.JsonStringEnumConverter isn't linker-safe
issue_context.body:
Most other converters in S.T.J. (as far as I know) are safe because their default constructors are referenced statically. However, if you use `JsonStringEnumConverter` like this:

```cs
[JsonConverter(typeof(JsonStringEnumConverter))]
public enum MyEnum { A, B, C }
```

then there is no static reference to `JsonStringEnumConverter`'s default constructor, so the linker will strip it out. Then at runtime it will fail when `JsonSerializerOptions.GetConverterFromAttribute` tries to call `Activator.CreateInstance(converterType)` (where `converterType = typeof(JsonStringEnumConverter)`). This was originally reported at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/19086

For Blazor 3.2.0, we'll put in a workaround into Blazor's built-in linker config. However it would make sense to fix the underlying issue in S.T.J. in the longer term.

### Suggested fix

Either `System.Text.Json.dll` should embed its own linker config file preserving the constructors for all converter types, or consider extending the set of types listed in `JsonSerializerOptions.DefaultSimpleConverters` to include an instantiation of `JsonStringEnumConverter` (or have any other static reference to its constructor).

This applies to all converter types that may be used at runtime. The only one I know of that's causing a problem is `JsonStringEnumConverter`, but I didn't exhaustively check that all the others are linker-safe too.
comments:
Another potential way to fix this is to add the correct dataflow analysis annotations (https://github.com/mono/linker/pull/988) to JsonConverter. Using the current names in that proposal, all we would need to add `[DynamicallyAccessedMembers(MemberKinds.DefaultConstructor)]` to `JsonConverterAttribute`, which would tell the linker to keep the default constructor on any type passed into `JsonConverter`.

/cc @vitek-karas @MichalStrehovsky @sbomer

Yes, we'll want to solve this through annotations - the fact that the other converters have their constructor rooted from elsewhere is hardly a contract one could rely on: they just _happen to work right now_. We are working on a linking solution that would let us guarantee things work after linking by construction (as opposed to "working thanks to luck").

review_comments: Why was this removed? Is the linker recognizing these dependencies now?

Yes - this situation is similar to the discussion in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/38216#discussion_r445670381/. Because there are `typeof` usages in the code, the linker can recognize these dependencies.
Don't we need the constructor as well on write?
No - we don't construct new objects during write. (Note that this is writing the objects to JSON)
These don't seem to have corresponding entries in the `ref` file. Or am I missing it?

This may be a bit of a stretch, but are we concerned that when we are testing `Deserialize` we are also calling `Serialize`? Could there ever be a bug where if the app ONLY called `Deserialize`, something was broken? But we are always doing both in our tests.

The intention of these collection tests is to exercise the warm-up code paths of the serializer which is the same for both serialization and deserialization, so we can test either side. Here, we are checking that the reflection-based dependencies like the collection converters, `CreateRange` methods for immutable collections, `Push`/`Enqueue` for `Stack`/`Queue` etc., are rooted when needed.

The tests for each serializer method overload are found in the `TrimmingTest\SerializerEntryPoint` directory. For each of these, we test a POCO and collection. Issues with serialization or deserialization specifically would be pointed out by these tests.
I don't think I understand why you need this?
I understand why you need it now. I'm not sure I agree with what we are doing here to be honest, but I'm fine if that is the direction we are going to take.

Yes, that is the direction we've decided to take. See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/36656#issuecomment-630345623

The other attributes in this folder already have it:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/8126962457be677cb8b9313d5d9f26849da77df2/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Diagnostics/CodeAnalysis/DynamicDependencyAttribute.cs#L17-L22

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/8126962457be677cb8b9313d5d9f26849da77df2/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Diagnostics/CodeAnalysis/NullableAttributes.cs#L9-L14

I see, honestly I don't fully agree with this approach (as opposed to having them available down level) since we probably want to allow library developers that target netstandard or < .NET5.0 to be able to annotate their libraries as well, specially if these will be libraries used for blazor wasm. Given the attribute implementation is fully netstandard2.0 compatible, I would opt instead for having compatibility packs (similar to what we did with AsyncInterfaces) for shipping the attributes down level so that we a) don't have to compile these attributes internally on a bunch of libraries and b) allow third party library writters to consume them. I don't want to push to much on doing this but just wanted to share my opinion 😄 cc: @stephentoub

@eerhardt I believe that I've asked this already but is there a requirement for us to also update the ref code with these attributes? I know that they only used on the linker fwith the actual implementation, but I'm not sure if we should add them to the refs so that other projects that depend on System.Text.Json throw linker warnings saying they have to add or propagate these attributes as well.
Good catch. Yes, we need to add these in the ref assemblies so when we link during the dotnet/runtime build the linker can see the attributes.

What about the other PRs where we've added attributes? Y suppose DynamicDependency ones don't really need to be propagated to the refs, but I believe we have added DynamicAccessedMembers attributes on other PRs as well.

> DynamicDependency ones don't really need to be propagated to the refs

Correct. Those are explicitly left out.

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/ecdb7f36e0d97e204194ee23a972160471b44622/eng/DefaultGenApiDocIds.txt#L10

> but I believe we have added DynamicAccessedMembers attributes on other PRs as well.

The ones that @MichalStrehovsky opened have updated the refs. e.g. https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/38331 and https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/38021.

We should update the `ref` assemblies on any place we've added but haven't updated the `ref` files.

> We should update the ref assemblies on any place we've added but haven't updated the ref files.

I'll scan through and make a PR to add them, if any.
